text.p: British drug discovery firm Chiroscience Group Plc said on Friday it expected significantly better results this year, boosted by its profitable ChiroTech unit and its new pact with U.S. group Schering-Plough Corp.
"Clearly the earnings this year will be significantly more than they were last year," chief executive Dr. John Padfield told Reuters in an interview.
Chiroscience posted an operating loss of 21.0 million stg last year compared to a loss of 13.1 million stg the previous year.
Padfield said results this year would be helped by a strong performance at its technical services operation, ChiroTech, which reported its first profit in the year ended on February 28.

The company should also begin to reap the benefits from the Schering-Plough deal, which is worth up to $38 million and involves developing PDE IV inhibitors to treat asthma. "The vast majority of that is money coming directly to the company over a period of the next four years," Padfield said, adding that "a couple of million" would go towards research and development.
He declined to be more specific about financial terms of the deal.
Chiroscience's shares surged nearly seven percent, rising 16p to 253.5 to rank among the top percentage gainers on the London Stock Exchange at 0905 GMT.
The company expected to report results by October from its Phase I trial examining PD IV inhibitor D4418 as an asthma treatment.
The inhibitors, which target the phosphodiesterase type IV enzyme, suppress the body's reaction to foreign substances during an asthma attack.
"Asthma is an overreaction to a challenge, and what these compounds do is dampen down that overreaction," said director of development Brian Gennery.

Chiroscience believe its PDE IV inhibitors, which will likely take the form of a pill, will avoid the side effects of nausea and vomiting that have hampered other companies' research on the treatment.

"What we're aiming to demonstrate in Phase I is that there's no nausea and vomiting, or if it occurs, it occurs at a very, very high dose where it wouldn't be a problem commercially," Padfield said, adding that animal studies indicated minimal side effects.
If successful, the company would start Phase II trials on D4418 in 1998/99.

Under the Schering-Plough deal, the companies also planned to develop PD IV inhibitors to treat other ailments, such as chronic bronchitis and arthritis. Regarding Chiroscience's finances, Padfield said the company had about 50 million stg of cash, which it was spending at a rate of about 25 million stg a year. "For this coming year our burn rate of roughly two million pounds (net) a month should be roughly the same as last year," he said.
"We have sufficient cash to meet our current business requirements. We have no current intention to return to the equity market for more cash," he added.
